title: How the Mighty Have Fallen: David's Lament
summary: Two days after David returns to Ziklag, an Amalekite arrives from the battlefield with Saul's crown and armband, claiming he killed the wounded king at Saul's own request. David and his men mourn, and David has the man executed for lifting his hand against the LORD's anointed. Then David sings a lament for Saul and Jonathan, the Song of the Bow, with its refrain: How the mighty have fallen.
story: Second Samuel begins where 1 Samuel ended, on the day Saul fell on Mount Gilboa, but it tells the news from David's side. David has just come back from defeating the Amalekites who raided Ziklag (1 Samuel 30), and now an Amalekite brings him the crown of Israel. Everything in the long story of David's rise has led to this moment: Saul, who hunted him for years, is dead, and the throne is open. A man hungry for power would have rejoiced. David tears his clothes, fasts, executes the messenger who claims credit for the killing, and composes one of the great elegies of the Bible. The chapter establishes the character of the new reign at its threshold. David will not receive the kingdom as a prize taken from Saul's corpse, and he will not let others win his favor by shedding blood for him.
historical:
The setting is Ziklag, David's base in the western Negev given him by Achish of Gath (1 Samuel 27:6), shortly after the Philistine victory on Gilboa, around 1010 BC. The Philistines now controlled much of the north, and Israel had no king, no army in the field, and no clear heir, since three of Saul's sons had died with him.

The Amalekite's account does not match the narrator's report in 1 Samuel 31, where Saul, wounded by archers, falls on his own sword and his armor-bearer, seeing him dead, does the same. Most interpreters conclude that the Amalekite found Saul's body, took the crown and armband, and invented the story of the mercy killing to win a reward from the man he expected to be king. Some suggest the two accounts preserve separate traditions, or that Saul's own attempt had not quite killed him. The chapter itself hints at the first view: the man's phrase I happened to be there is suspicious, and he is an Amalekite, a member of the people David has just fought. Either way, David judges him by his own testimony.
cultural:
Tearing one's clothes, putting dust on the head, weeping, and fasting until evening were standard signs of grief in Israel. The messenger arrives already dressed as a mourner, perhaps sincerely, perhaps to play the part. The crown (a royal diadem) and the band worn on the arm were insignia of kingship; bringing them to David was a way of saying he was the new king and deserved thanks for it.

The man calls himself the son of a foreigner, using the word for a resident alien living in Israel under its protection and its laws. That status meant he could not plead ignorance of what the anointed king meant to Israel. Laments for fallen leaders were a known form of song, and this one was to be taught to the people of Judah. It was preserved in the Book of Jashar, a lost collection of poetry also cited in Joshua 10:13, apparently gathering heroic songs of Israel's early wars. Gath and Ashkelon, named in verse 20, were two of the five Philistine cities, and the daughters of the Philistines would have celebrated victory with songs and dances, as Israel's women once did for David (1 Samuel 18:6-7).
literary: The chapter has two halves: a narrative of the messenger (verses 1-16) and the lament (17-27). The narrative is built on repeated questions from David, each drawing out more from the man until his own words convict him. The lament is Hebrew poetry of great artistry, framed by the refrain “How the mighty have fallen” at its opening (verse 19), middle (verse 25), and close (verse 27). It moves from the public grief of Israel for its king to David's private grief for his friend. It never mentions God or Saul's sins, and it praises Saul for his courage and for the prosperity he brought. It curses the mountains of Gilboa as if the land itself should mourn. The final stanza turns to Jonathan in the first person, “I grieve for you, Jonathan, my brother”, the most intimate lines in the book.

outline.t: The lament introduced: the Song of the Bow
The lament for Saul and Jonathan

doctrines.note: David's question, “Why were you not afraid to lift your hand to destroy the LORD's anointed?”, sums up the conviction he has held throughout his outlaw years. The anointed king belongs to God, and no one advances by shedding his blood. The same reverence for the anointed runs forward into Israel's hope for the Messiah.

The new kingdom begins with grief, not triumph. David refuses to profit from Saul's death and honors him publicly. The chapter shows that the way power is received shapes the kind of rule that follows.
The lament gives Scripture's permission to grieve fully, even for a flawed person, and to put grief into words before God and the people. Biblical faith does not hurry past loss; it laments.

words.note: Gibbor, mighty man or warrior, a word for heroes of battle. It appears five times, most memorably in the refrain How the mighty have fallen. The word honors Saul and Jonathan as true warriors, whatever Saul's failures, and the refrain's grief lies in the gap between their strength and their end.

Tsevi, beauty or glory. The same Hebrew word also means gazelle, and some translators read the opening line as the gazelle of Israel lies slain, a picture of swift and graceful warriors that fits the lament's later image of men swifter than eagles. Either way the word names what Israel has lost: its splendor.

Ahavah, love. David says Jonathan's love to him surpassed the love of women. The word covers the whole range of love in the Old Testament, from God's covenant love and the love of friends to romantic and political loyalty. Jonathan had loved David as himself (1 Samuel 18:1-3) and had given up his own claim to the throne for him, and David honors that self-giving love here.

Qun, to chant a lament, a funeral dirge. The same kind of lament (qinah) became a recognized form in Israel's poetry, heard in the prophets and in the book of Lamentations. David's lament for Saul and Jonathan is one of the Old Testament's great examples.

christ: David's refusal to seize the throne through Saul's death, and his public mourning for the man who tried to kill him, show a king who loves his enemy. Jesus, the son of David, taught his followers to love their enemies (Matthew 5:44) and himself wept over Jerusalem, the city that would reject him (Luke 19:41). The link is one of character, not a prediction in the text. The chapter also shows that God's kingdom does not advance by the kind of violence the Amalekite offered. The kingdom of the Messiah would come not through a rival's blood but through the Messiah's own.

hard.q: What was the relationship between David and Jonathan?
hard.a: Some modern readers take David's words, “your love to me was extraordinary, surpassing the love of women”, as evidence of a romantic or sexual relationship. Most interpreters, ancient and modern, read it as the language of deep covenant friendship. They note that the Hebrew root for love here is used widely, including for political loyalty (Hiram loved David, 1 Kings 5:1) and the love of the people for David (1 Samuel 18:16); that the friendship was formalized by covenant (1 Samuel 18:3, 20:16-17); that the narrative shows no hint of sexual relationship; and that the lament's comparison is about loyalty that cost Jonathan his claim to a throne. Readers weighing the passage should notice that David's sexual history elsewhere in Samuel is described frankly, and nothing like it is described here. What is beyond dispute is the depth of the bond: Jonathan's love was sacrificial and faithful, and David grieves it as the greatest human loyalty he had known.

questions: David mourned sincerely for a king who had tried to kill him. What would it take for you to grieve honestly for someone who wronged you?
The Amalekite expected a reward for claiming Saul's death. Where are people tempted to win favor by bringing down someone else?
David wrote his grief into a song for others to learn. What place does lament have in your own prayer and in your church's worship?
